    Changelog

    Source: NEWS.md

    tidyvisor (development version)

    • Three new tools from current statistical practice, each returning advice with its reasons and a sentence for the paper:

      • tv_check_model() checks a fitted model with scaled residuals from simulations of the model (Dunn and Smyth 1996; the DHARMa method of Hartig), with tests of uniformity, dispersion, zero inflation and outliers, for lm(), glm(), MASS::glm.nb(), lme4 and glmmTMB models.
      • tv_equivalence() tests whether a difference is small enough to ignore, with two one-sided tests (TOST; Schuirmann 1987, Lakens 2017), so “no difference” is never claimed from a non-significant test.
      • tv_evalue() gives the E-value of an observational estimate (VanderWeele and Ding 2017), the strength of unmeasured confounding that would explain it away, for risk, odds and hazard ratios and standardised mean differences. Values match the EValue package.

    • A third companion: tidyepidemio (epidemiology). tidyvisor() hands it case counts, exposures and outcomes, and its results (ratios, Rt, growth, diagnostic accuracy, surveillance alerts, standardised effects, survival curves); advisors() lists it. tidymapr keeps the spatial side of epidemics and no longer claims case counts without locations.

    • tidyepidemio is in Suggests and Remotes, the installation steps include it, and the package description names all three companions. The package language is now New Zealand English (Language: en-NZ).

    • Publication advice. Every interpretation of a test or a model ends with a section “For the paper”:

      • a sentence for the Results with the numbers in the usual order (“count differed among levels of spray (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test; H(5) = 54.7, p < 0.001)”); factor levels in words against the reference level, and ratios or odds ratios for log and logit models;
      • the figure to make, with ggplot2 or ggeffects code that uses the data’s own names and ggsave() at a journal column width, and the rules for journal figures (raw data shown, units, colour-blind-safe palettes, vector formats, text size);
      • the table to make (with gtsummary or broom code for models), and what the Methods must state (test or model, software and versions). Assumption tests are flagged as checks, not results.

    • tv_practice("report") adds advice on figures to a journal’s specification, lean tables, reporting each statistical result in full, and describing the analysis so it can be repeated.

    • After an overall test, the interpretation says what to do next in a new section, “After the overall test”:

      • significant, with three or more groups: go on to post hoc comparisons, with the method that suits the test (pairwise Wilcoxon or Dunn after Kruskal-Wallis, Games-Howell or Tukey after ANOVA, cell residuals or pairwise proportions after a chi-squared test) and code that uses the data’s own column names;
      • not significant: do not test every pair, which is a search for something significant; report the effect size and the difference the study could have detected;
      • two groups: no post hoc tests are needed; report the effect size. For lm(), glm(), aov(), lmer(), glmer() and glmmTMB() fits, each factor with three or more levels is tested with drop1(): when it matters, its levels are compared with emmeans (Tukey, or Dunnett against a control), and within each level of the other factor when they interact.

    • tidyvisor() reads an aov() fit as the linear model it is (it failed before).

    • tv_save() writes advice and interpretations to a text or Markdown file, and format() returns them as text. In the RStudio console the advice could not be captured with capture.output() or sink().

    • Clearer printed advice:

      • tv_power(): “Needed: 42 samples per group (84 in total)”, and the sensitivity lines read “162 samples per group”; “an 80% chance”.
      • Headings name the question: “good research practice”, “how many samples?”, “is the design sound?”.
      • Degrees of freedom of a test print as whole numbers (df = 5).
      • The design audit names each group: “Diet 1: 20, Diet 2: 10”.
      • Placeholders in suggested code are marked, e.g. delta = <difference to detect>.

    • Website: a full user guide in eight chapters (research practice, power, assumptions, regression, mixed and additive models, Bayesian models, community and spatial ecology, writing an advisor) and two tutorials that follow whole studies from the question to the report.

    • tidyvisor is now a general statistical advisor for any field:

      • tv_practice(): good research practice for planning, data collection, analysis and reporting, by kind of study, with the reporting guideline for the field (CONSORT, STROBE, ARRIVE, PRISMA, STARD, ODMAP, TTEE).
      • advise(data, question = "design"): a data audit (missing values, duplicated rows, constant columns, numbers stored as text, the unit of replication and pseudoreplication, treatments confounded with time, unbalanced groups) with the suggested analysis. tidyvisor() falls back on it when no specialised advisor recognises the data, so it always answers.

    • A website at https://tidyvisor.in4metrix.dev/, laid out like those of tidydiversity and tidymapr, with a Get started page and three guides: research practice and study design, power analysis, and assumption checks.

    • README: installation lists tidyvisor first, then tidydiversity and tidymapr, saying what each does.

    • Power analysis before fieldwork: tv_power(), or advise(pilot, question = "power", ...) with pilot data. It gives the samples, traps, pairs, observations or sites needed to detect a given effect, for two or more groups, paired designs, proportions, counts (Poisson and negative binomial), regression, correlation and samples nested in sites (with the intra-class correlation), with a sensitivity table and the code.

    • Two guides: checking assumptions and choosing the test, and power analysis before fieldwork.

    • Assumption checks and what to do when they fail:

      • New group-comparison advice (question = "compare", or give response and group, with paired for repeated measurements). It checks normality, skewness, outliers, equal spread and whether the spread grows with the mean, then recommends the test those checks support: Student or Welch t-test and ANOVA, a log scale, trimmed means (Yuen), a rank test (Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis), a permutation test, or a Poisson or negative binomial GLM for counts. The alternatives come with their code.
      • tidyvisor() now explains any classical test result (htest): the statistic, p-value, estimate and interval, what the test does not show, and what to do next.
      • The interpretation of a linear model ends with “What to do next”: a log or Box-Cox transformation, a Gamma GLM, robust standard errors, robust regression (MASS::rlm()), a count GLM, or rank and permutation alternatives, depending on which checks failed.

    • The vegan advisor covers the rest of the CANOCO toolkit: restricted permutations for blocks (blocks) and time series (time), canonical variate analysis for groups of sites, variation partitioning between environment and space (lon, lat; tidymapr::geo_varpart()), and trait-environment analysis with dc-CA or RLQ (traits).

    tidyvisor 0.2.0

    • New built-in advisors for six modelling packages, each with advice before fitting and an interpretation after it:
      • lme4 (question = "mixed", or give random): checks the grouping factors, chooses lmer(), glmer() or glmer.nb(), and explains fixed effects, random-effect standard deviations, the intra-class correlation, singular fits and convergence.
      • glmmTMB (question = "zero_inflation"): negative binomial and zero-inflated mixed models, with the probability of a structural zero.
      • mgcv (question = "smooth", or give smooth): additive models, each smooth explained by its effective degrees of freedom, with basis (k) and concurvity checks.
      • vegan (question = "vegan"): chooses RDA or CCA from the gradient length, NMDS, PERMANOVA and its dispersion check; explains metaMDS() stress, constrained ordinations with permutation tests, adonis2(), betadisper() and envfit().
      • brms (question = "bayesian"): family, weakly informative priors, prior and posterior predictive checks; explains effects with credible intervals and the probability of their direction, group-level standard deviations, and R-hat, effective sample size and divergences.
      • aods3 (question = "overdispersion"): beta-binomial and negative binomial models, with the overdispersion parameter explained.
    • tidyvisor() sends results that are also data frames (an adonis2() table) to interpret().
    • interpret() uses the advisor for the most specific class, so a gam (which is also a glm) goes to the mgcv advisor.
    • New built-in advisor for linear and generalised linear models (question = "regression", and any fitted lm or glm). Before fitting, it chooses the family and link from the kind of response (continuous, counts, binary, proportions, positive and skewed), checks counts for overdispersion and excess zeros, the number of observations and events per parameter, collinear predictors and missing values, and gives the model code. After fitting, it reports the fit, each effect on its natural scale (change per unit, rate ratio or odds ratio) with confidence intervals, and diagnostics: overdispersion, non-constant variance, non-normal residuals, influential observations, collinearity and separation.

    tidyvisor 0.1.0

    • First release. tidyvisor is the statistical advisor shared by tidydiversity and tidymapr, moved into a package of its own so that one tidyvisor() serves both, whichever is loaded.
    • tidyvisor() advises on data (advise()) and interprets fitted results (interpret()).
    • register_advisor() lets any package add an advisor; advisors() lists them. Advisors for tidydiversity (community ecology) and tidymapr (spatial ecology) are built in and used when those packages are installed.
